newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan's rival ethnic factions keep Karachi tense.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan's rival ethnic factions keep Karachi tense.

text.p: A dozen Pakistani youngsters finger their Kalashnikov rifles outside the main office of an ethnic party in Karachi's troubled Landhi area.
The imposing building, known as the White House, is the headquarters of the splinter MQM-Haqiqi faction, which is feuding with the mainstream Mohajir National Movement (MQM).
Violence between the two has mounted in recent weeks after a few months of relative peace in Pakistan's biggest city in the run-up to elections on February 3.
Nightly gunfire reverberates through parts of District East, where the two factions are fighting a bitter turf war.
At least 30 people have died in tit-for-tat killings since the national and provincial assembly elections and many people fear the feud may turn into full-scale clashes.
"Both groups are well-armed and the situation could worsen any time as they strive to control various Karachi localities," said a senior police officer, who asked not to be named.
SPLINTER GROUP STILL ACTIVE DESPITE ELECTION DEFEAT
MQM-Haqiqi was routed at the polls, but witnesses say its militants still hold sway in several volatile areas.
"We tightened security at our head office after killings of our workers and an attack on our chairman Afaq Ahmed by the MQM in the past few weeks," said Younus Khan of MQM-Haqiqi.
The mainstream MQM, led by London-based Altaf Hussain, denies responsibility for any violence and accuses the MQM-Haqiqi of obstructing its workers and representatives.
"It's most unfortunate that even elected representatives of the MQM can't go to their constituencies to serve people because of the presence of Haqiqi terrorists," said MQM spokesman Shoaib Bukhari.

The MQM, part of the government that took power in the southern province of Sindh in February, demands action against MQM-Haqiqi under an agreement with its coalition partner, the Pakistan Muslim League led by Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif.
MQM-Haqiqi took over parts of Karachi on June 19, 1992 when the army cracked down against the MQM, an operation pursued vigorously by then-premier Benazir Bhutto's government from 1993 to 1996.
The MQM-Haqiqi is widely believed to have been created by Pakistan's military at start of army operations against the MQM.
Bhutto held the MQM responsible for most of the violence in Karachi, capital of Sindh province, where more than 2,000 people were killed in 1995 and about 800 last year.
The MQM speaks for Urdu-speakers who migrated from India at partition in 1947 at the end of British colonial rule in the Asian subcontinent.
It has accused the government of letting security forces kill many MQM activists in cold blood.
MQM SUSPECTS RANGERS OF PROTECTING RIVALS
The MQM says the military still wants to keep MQM-Haqiqi in existence.
"Every time elections were held, our party swept the polls even in Haqiqi-controlled areas, but there is an element in the establishment which wants to keep Haqiqi alive," Bukhari said.
"We have no complaint against Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif. He sincerely wants to solve our problems," he added.
The MQM says MQM-Haqiqi has held onto certain districts in Karachi with the support of paramilitary rangers, part of Pakistan's security forces.
MQM-Haqiqi says police started a crackdown against its workers after the MQM joined the Sindh government in February.

"They have arrested dozens of our workers to please the MQM," said Haqiqi leader Ahmed. "Our opponents enter various areas carrying arms under police protection. But we expected this after the MQM won elections."
Newly-appointed Karachi police chief Mohammad Iqbal said his force was determined to seize all illegal weapons, but did not favour one group over another.

"We have no political considerations. All the political groups have illegal weapons and we are trying to recover them," he said, adding that police had arrested 60 to 70 activists of various political parties for illegal possession of weapons.
MQM-Haqiqi says police have arrested more than 300 of its workers in the past few weeks.
NO COMPROMISE IN SIGHT
Chances of reconciling the two factions appear remote.
"There can be no compromise with the terrorists and we demand proper action against them," Bukhari said.
Ahmed said MQM leader Hussain did not believe in co-existence and could not tolerate any rivals.
"He wants to wipe us out completely. That's why we have to keep weapons to defend ourselves," Ahmed said.
"We will not stop MQM workers if they come unarmed, but if they come with weapons we will resist."
